summary:
South Dakota restricts transgender people from using bathrooms, locker rooms and changing areas matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings under House Bill 1259, signed by Governor Larry Rhoden on 20 March 2025 and announced the following day. The law took effect on 1 July 2025 and passed the state House 49-21. Its scope covers state-run facilities, primarily K-12 schools and state colleges, including off-campus activities. It is the first facilities restriction of its kind to be enacted in the state, after comparable bills failed in 2016, 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022.

The law's "reasonable accommodation" clause and the floor debate around it raised the prospect that incarcerated transgender people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply.

No South Dakota statute explicitly prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Federal law supplies the only backstop: Title VII employment protection as construed in Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) and federal hate-crime prosecution under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act.

Identity documents are closed to gender-marker change. On 5 March 2026 the South Dakota Supreme Court ruled that a transgender person cannot amend the sex designation on a South Dakota birth certificate to reflect gender identity, affirming the denial of Sigrid Nielsen's September 2024 petition to change the marker from male to female and holding that a change is permitted only to correct an error made at birth. A legal gender change on a driver's licence or state ID remains available by court order or a physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery, and on a birth certificate by court order, photo ID, application and fee.

Gender-affirming care for people under 18 is banned under House Bill 1080, passed in February 2023 and signed on 13 February 2023. The law required prior puberty-blocker or hormone treatment to be systematically reduced, ending no later than 31 December 2023, and authorises affected people to sue until age 25 or within three years of discovering an injury.

An advocacy legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 lists South Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the most severe bills.

State institutions have also acted against transgender health provision directly. On 16 December 2022 South Dakota terminated The Transformation Project's $136,000 federally funded Community Health Worker contract for LGBTQ+ and transgender community health in Sioux Falls. To settle the organisation's discrimination lawsuit, Health Secretary Melissa Magstadt issued an apology letter on 17 January 2024 acknowledging the termination and differential treatment compared with other Community Health Worker contractors, affirming equal treatment under law regardless of race, colour, national origin, religion, disability, age or sex; the state paid $300,000 covering attorney fees, committed not to discriminate against the Project in violation of state or federal law in any services, programmes or activities, and allowed the retention of community health worker Jack Fonder.
tangentialFactors:
Transgender participation in female school sports was restricted by executive order in March 2021, after Governor Kristi Noem declined to sign a broader legislative ban over college-sports concerns, and then by statute signed on 4 February 2022 and effective 1 July 2022; the ACLU threatened federal litigation.

Earlier legislative attempts set the pattern. A March 2016 bill requiring transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching birth sex was vetoed by Governor Dennis Daugaard, and House Bill 1108, barring K-7 instruction on gender identity and expression, passed the House on 12 February 2019 but failed in the Senate on 29 March 2019.

A March 2021 law signed by Governor Kristi Noem allows businesses to deny goods or services to LGBTQ people on the basis of owners' purported religious beliefs, and S.B. 149, signed by Governor Dennis Daugaard on 10 March 2017, permits taxpayer-funded foster care and adoption agencies to deny services to LGBT people, including qualified LGBT prospective parents, on religious grounds.
localsOnly:
Protection below the state level is patchy. Oglala Lakota County and the cities of Sioux Falls, Vermillion and Brookings provide limited public-employee or, in Brookings' March 2018 ordinance, comprehensive employment, housing and public-accommodations protections; Minnehaha County, Spearfish and Watertown also provide limited public-employee protections. In September 2019 the Oglala Sioux Tribal Council passed hate-crime legislation protecting LGBT and two-spirit individuals by a 14-2-1 vote.

Marriage between two people regardless of sex has been recognised in South Dakota since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, superseding a November 2006 constitutional amendment and statutes defining marriage as between a man and a woman and barring recognition of other unions. The change followed Rosenbrahn v. Daugaard, filed 22 May 2014, in which Judge Karen Schreier ruled for the plaintiffs on 12 January 2015, with the ruling stayed pending appeal.

Adoption law does not specify rules for single individuals or married same-sex couples; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation with non-genetic married mothers recognised after donor insemination, and gay male couples may use surrogacy with pre-birth orders, but S.J. 746, enacted in May 2017, permits agencies to refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions.
outOfScopeNotes:
How South Dakota's 2025 facilities law is enforced in state custody is unresolved: the enacted text does not specify how the "reasonable accommodation" requirement is to be met, and the solitary-confinement prospect was raised in floor debate rather than written into the statute.

Whether the driver's licence and state ID gender-change procedure remains operative after the March 2026 birth-certificate ruling is not sourced; the two concern different documents and the ruling addressed birth certificates only.

The document-change procedures described here are drawn from a reference article on LGBTQ rights in South Dakota and have not been confirmed against current state agency guidance.

The July 2026 legal-risk ranking is an advocacy assessment built on a bill-severity rubric, not a legal determination, and its placement of South Dakota should be read as a legislative-trend indicator rather than a statement of enforceable law.
